summary:
Sections 365 and 365A of the Penal Code criminalise same-sex activity. Section 365 covers "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" and applies to men; Section 365A covers "gross indecency" and was amended in 1995 to reach women, so both provisions now apply to men and women. The maximum penalty is ten years' imprisonment. Where an offence under these sections is committed by a person over 18 against a person under 16, the penalty rises to ten to twenty years' rigorous imprisonment.

Prosecutions are limited. The Canada Immigration and Refugee Board's January 2012 research found no convictions under the articles, and Outright International's March 2026 overview describes prosecutions as limited. The provisions nonetheless structure everyday policing. The US State Department's country report documents police harassment of LGBT persons, and the 2012 research found that criminalisation "paves the way for police and anti-gay groups to brand all lesbian, bisexual, transgendered persons as perverts and criminals". Advocacy groups report that police routinely ignore complaints from LGBTQ victims, particularly those involving sexual violence or blackmail, citing Article 365 as justification, and human rights organisations have documented police using the threat of arrest to assault, harass and extort LGBTQIA individuals.

The International Commission of Jurists' August 2023 opinion piece by Mathuri Thamilmaran identifies the Sri Lanka Police as the foremost perpetrators of human-rights violations against LGBTI individuals, noting that in the months preceding publication both the Police and the Human Rights Commission of Sri Lanka acknowledged this. The piece argues that administrative circulars are insufficient without legal reform.

Authorities use forced anal and vaginal examinations to seek evidence of same-sex conduct, a practice widely condemned as torture. There are no comprehensive anti-discrimination protections covering sexual orientation or gender identity.

Legal gender recognition is possible through a certification process. A 2016 Ministry of Health circular, issued following a March 2015 complaint facilitated by the Human Rights Commission of Sri Lanka, established the issuance of gender recognition certificates to transgender people; the recognised identity card has been issued under this circular since June 2016. No surgical intervention is legally required, though the bureaucratic certification may be onerous to obtain.

Sri Lanka's Prisons Department has no dedicated transgender housing. In October 2024, Media Spokesperson and Commissioner Gamini Dissanayake stated that current prison facilities make giving transgender prisoners their own space impossible, with separate accommodation planned only for prisons built in the future. Placement is decided case by case: transgender detainees holding the recognised identity card are accommodated according to their preferred gender where possible, while those without it undergo a doctor's assessment of whether they can be considered transgender before placement, with the inmate's preference feeding the decision. Officials have stated concern about people accused of sex offences identifying as transgender to enter female housing with born-male offenders, given as a reason for resisting gender-based placement. Placement by birth sex is the practical default under the current male and female ward system, with a medicalised, discretionary exception process and no statutory placement rule. The Committee for Protecting Rights of Prisoners has asked that future prisons give transgender and non-binary inmates a separate, chosen space, including possible space within prison hospitals.

Gender-affirming surgery is relatively inaccessible because many hospitals lack the highly specialised surgical units and staff required. A physician interviewed for Human Rights Watch's 2016 report 'All Five Fingers are Not the Same' said Sri Lankan doctors were often unfamiliar with surgical treatments for transgender patients. Patients report meeting ignorance, curiosity and even ridicule from medical staff when seeking gender-confirming care, and some avoid public hospitals and clinics as a result, raising treatment costs; obtaining hormone therapy is described as similarly fraught. The National Blood Transfusion Service bars men who have sex with men from donating blood, classifying male same-sex intercourse as "risky behaviour" alongside drug use and having multiple partners.

Sri Lankan family law does not recognise same-sex marriages, same-sex civil unions, or provide equal rights to same-sex live-in couples; the marriage law dates from colonial times. A 2023 report found 69% of the population opposed legalising same-sex unions, with 60% strongly opposed. In March 2022, SJB MP Rohini Kumari Wijerathna tabled a bill to ban conversion therapy, which she said the government failed to support as of July 2024; despite professional college ethics, doctors are reportedly still sought by families to administer "treatment" to LGBTQ family members.

The UK Home Office's September 2024 Country Policy and Information Note on Sri Lanka assesses risk from state and non-state actors, protection, internal relocation and certification for LGBT+ asylum claims. A joint UPR stakeholder report by EQUAL GROUND, Northwestern CIHR and GIHR for Sri Lanka's third cycle documents criminalisation and violations against LGBTIQ individuals.

Official posture is mixed. In March 2021, President Gotabaya Rajapaksa tweeted that he was determined to secure everybody's right to live with dignity regardless of sexuality and gender, which the Financial Times called the first such public acknowledgement by a South Asian head of state. A 2021 Social Scientists Association poll found 72.5% of respondents believed LGBT people should not be punished for their sexual identity, 65% said an LGBT person can do a job as well as anyone else, and 51.4% would support rights legislation. In August 2021 a video of a homophobic counsellor caused controversy; the College of Psychiatrists clarified that modern medicine does not consider homosexuality an illness and called for decriminalisation, noting that counsellors are not regulated and do not require degrees. Community organisations include Companions on a Journey (1994), the Women's Support Group (1999) and Equal Ground, though Section 365 remains cited to justify police harassment and moral policing of LGBTQ people in public and private settings.
tangentialFactors:
The Human Dignity Trust's country profile on Sri Lanka was not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying profile documents Sri Lanka's criminalisation of same-sex activity.

The Catholic Church in Sri Lanka does not recognise same-sex marriages, with Cardinal Malcolm Ranjith stating that same-sex marriages "are not a human right". The influential Asgiriya Buddhist chapter has backed rights extension and constitutional amendment, and politicians from both major parties have expressed support for LGBTQ rights. A 2018 Equality Fund survey found 12% of respondents were LGBTQI. No youth-specific care-access findings appear in the source text.
